item.title: Liberty Media founder sells voting power of F1's parent company
item.description: Liberty Media founder and ex-chairman John Malone has sold his significant voting power in F1's parent company
item.dc:creator: Samarth Kanal
item.content:encoded:
Liberty Media founder and ex-chairman John Malone has sold his significant voting power in Formula 1's parent company.

Malone founded Liberty Media in 1991 and stepped down as chairman of the board in 2026, nine years after Liberty Media acquired F1 for $4.6billion USD (£3.4bn).

Malone was the most significant voting shareholder of Liberty Media until early November 2026 when Liberty Media announced that it had purchased Malone's 'high-vote' stock and exchanged it for 'low-vote' stock, essentially diluting Malone's voting power from around 48% to 3%.

Liberty Media purchased the high-vote stock after Malone received "a number of unsolicited offers from third parties" to acquire it.

The transaction effectively eliminates the transfer of Malone's voting power to a third party and strengthens Liberty Media shareholders' power in voting matters - such as a sale of F1.

In 2025, Malone said on the Opening Bid Unfiltered finance podcast that Liberty would be open to a sale of F1 - with the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund (PIF) among F1's then-touted suitors.

item.title: What we learned from an unexpected MotoGP cameo
item.description: Jake Dixon's factory Honda MotoGP cameo in the Qatar GP was a marvellous advert - both for Dixon and for the wider world of motorcycle racing
item.dc:creator: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded:
Jake Dixon's cameo as a factory Honda MotoGP rider in the Qatar Grand Prix was a marvellous advert - both for Dixon himself and for the wider world of motorcycle racing.

Yes, it was approximately 50 light-years removed from the wildcard heroics of yesteryear, from the days when a World Superbike regular like Troy Bayliss could show up to a MotoGP round and just...win.

Dixon didn't win, nor was he particularly close. But in the modern MotoGP reality of hyper-specialisation, and a grid of riders whose pre-MotoGP CVs are incredible top to bottom and whose current machines are separated by less than ever in terms of performance, he gave a fantastic account of himself showing up at late notice at Lusail as the replacement for the ill Joan Mir.
